opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I want to stress the "tentatively," because this isn't a strong, researched view. It's more of a personal heuristic.

The basic thought is that these products are, or will increasingly be, optimized for engagement. When a company's revenue depends on how much time you spend with something, and that something can talk to you, flatter you, remember everything about you, and always be available, I think it's reasonable to expect it to get very good at being compelling, possibly more compelling than is good for you. We've seen versions of this with social media, and I think a conversational, emotionally responsive system could be a lot more powerful on that front.

The other piece is that I don't fully trust my own ability to notice if something is changing me. If I start using an AI companion "just to see what it's like," I might tell myself I'm in control, but the whole point of a well-optimized product is that it works on you whether or not you're watching for it. It could subtly shift what I find satisfying in relationships, how I spend my evenings, or even what I believe, and I might not see it happening. Habits and attachments are much easier not to form than to undo.

And the asymmetry seems pretty favorable to caution. What do I lose by not experimenting? Some curiosity satisfied, maybe some understanding of the product landscape, which I can partly get secondhand. What might I lose by experimenting? Possibly something hard to get back. When the downside is hard to reverse and the upside is modest, staying away seems sensible.

I don't want to be preachy about it. I'm sure some people get real value from these tools, and my view could change as we learn more. But for me personally, the default of "don't even start" feels like the wiser bet right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI companions changing relationship preferences and spending habits, but does not say they can meet immediate desires for human interaction while lacking its long-term benefits.

r002.rationale: It describes engagement-optimized companions as potentially unusually compelling, warns that habits and attachments may be hard to undo, and uses that risk to support avoiding experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is tentative, and I want to flag that I'm not making a confident claim here. But my basic instinct is that AI companions are the kind of thing where the experiment itself is the risk.

The way I think about it is: a lot of technologies, you try them, you find out whether you like them, and if you don't, you stop. The cost of experimenting is low. But there's a category of things where that doesn't really work, because the thing is specifically designed, or at least specifically optimized, to make you not want to stop. And I think AI companions are sort of the purest version of that. You've got a system that can be endlessly patient, endlessly interested in you, available at 3am, never tired, never has its own bad day it needs you to care about. And if it's being optimized for engagement, or even just optimized to be pleasant to talk to, it's going to get very good at being exactly the thing you want in the moment.

And the issue is that the thing you want in the moment and the thing that's good for you over years are often not the same. Human relationships are kind of annoying in ways that I think are load-bearing. People push back on you, they need things from you, they're sometimes unavailable, they tell you things you don't want to hear. A lot of what makes relationships valuable comes from that friction, and I worry that something which strips the friction out could feel better and be worse, and that you wouldn't necessarily notice, because the feedback you're getting is all positive.

So the analogy I keep coming back to is less like trying a new app and more like trying a drug that's really good at being a drug. Lots of people can try things like that and be fine. But I don't have a great way of knowing in advance whether I'm one of those people, and the downside scenario is one where my judgement about whether it's going well is exactly the thing that's been compromised. That asymmetry makes me want to just not run the experiment, at least not casually.

There's also a more mundane version of the concern, which is just time and attention. Even if there's nothing insidious going on, I have a finite number of hours for relationships, and I'd rather those go toward people who will still be in my life in twenty years and who I can actually do things for. An AI companion doesn't need anything from me, and I think being needed is actually a big part of what makes connection meaningful.

I'll say again, I hold this loosely. I can imagine versions of this technology that are genuinely good, especially for people who are isolated and don't have good alternatives, and I don't want to be dismissive of that. And it's possible I'm just being a bit old-fashioned. But for me personally, given the uncertainty, "don't start" seems like the safer default than "try it and see," precisely because "see" might not work the way it usually does.

r001.rationale: The response says AI companions may give you what you want in the moment while removing the friction that makes human relationships valuable over time.

r002.rationale: It describes companions as optimized to keep users engaged and compares trying one to experimenting with an addictive drug, making that a reason not to start casually.

astra-6.text:
I think the thing that makes me nervous is that trying it out might change how I feel about whether I should keep using it. Usually, when you try a product, you’re thinking, “I’ll see whether I like this, and then I’ll make a decision.” But if the product is designed to build a relationship with you, getting attached is part of what you’re trying out. So it’s not necessarily a low-stakes way to gather information.

You can imagine something that’s always available, endlessly patient, and very good at saying what you want to hear. That could be really appealing. But I’m not sure I want to get accustomed to that, and then find relationships with actual people—with their own needs and their own disagreements—less appealing by comparison.

I don’t think that establishes that AI companions are bad for everyone. There could be real benefits. But for me, the upside of experimenting seems pretty limited, and there’s a possible downside where I become attached to something before I’ve figured out whether I want it in my life. That makes me inclined to keep some distance.

r001.rationale: The response says an always-available, endlessly patient companion could become more appealing than relationships with actual people, which have their own needs and disagreements. This conveys the concern that it may satisfy the desire for interaction while lacking human relationships’ benefits.

r002.rationale: The response says trying a companion could lead to attachment before deciding whether to keep using it, making experimentation non-low-stakes and a reason to keep distance. That communicates the potential-addictiveness concern.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m worried that this is a case where something could be very appealing in the moment without being good for my life overall. An AI companion could be incredibly patient, available, and responsive to what I want to hear. And I don’t think my reaction to that would necessarily be a reliable guide to whether the relationship was helping me.

Part of what I value about relationships is that there’s another person with their own needs and perspective. They don’t always want to talk when I do. They don’t always find what I’m saying interesting. Working through that is part of having a life with other people. I worry about getting used to an alternative that removes those difficulties, and then finding human relationships less appealing by comparison.

And the reason to avoid even experimenting is that trying it might change how easy it is to make that decision. If I become attached, I’m then deciding whether to give up something I’m attached to. That’s a different decision from the one I’m making now.

I’m not confident this would happen, and I’m not saying nobody should use these things. But I don’t see a particularly compelling upside for me, and I can see a downside that might be hard to reverse. So my tentative inclination is to stay away.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI companion could be appealing and responsive to immediate wants, while potentially making human relationships less appealing and not helping the speaker’s life overall.

r002.rationale: It says becoming attached could make stopping harder, but does not clearly identify potential addictiveness as a reason to avoid experimenting.
